title: The skull, maxilla, mandible & TMJ
blurb: The bones of the skull and jaws, the landmarks of the mandible, and how the jaw joint moves.
question: Near the end of a long appointment a patient yawns widely and suddenly cannot close their mouth. They are distressed and pointing in front of their ears. Which joint is involved, what has happened to it, and which bony landmarks does the dentist need to understand?

teach.body: The skull has two parts. The cranium is the box that protects the brain. The facial skeleton forms the face, the eye sockets, the nose and the jaws. Most skull bones are locked together by fixed, fibrous joints called sutures. The one big exception is the mandible (lower jaw): it is the only skull bone that moves, through the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) on each side.

children.sub: Frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid

children.label: Face (14)
children.sub: 2 maxillae, mandible, 2 zygomatic, 2 nasal, 2 palatine, vomer and others

teach.caption: The temporal bone matters most in dentistry: it holds the socket of the jaw joint. The zygomatic bone and arch form the cheekbone.

teach.body: The maxilla is a pair of bones joined at the midline. Its alveolar process holds the upper teeth, and its palatine processes form the front of the hard palate (the palatine bones form the back). Behind the last molar is the maxillary tuberosity. Inside each maxilla is a large air space, the maxillary sinus. The roots of the upper premolars and molars sit close to its floor, which is why an upper molar extraction can open into the sinus (an oro-antral communication) and why sinusitis can feel like toothache.

teach.h: Teeth whose roots lie near the maxillary sinus
teach.caption: Upper premolars and molars. The dentist warns patients not to blow their nose hard after an upper molar extraction if a sinus opening is suspected.

teach.body: The mandible is horseshoe-shaped. The horizontal body carries the lower teeth in its alveolar process. At the back, a vertical plate of bone called the ramus rises on each side, meeting the body at the angle. The top of the ramus splits into two processes: the condyle at the back, which forms the jaw joint, and the coronoid process at the front, where the temporalis muscle attaches. The dip between them is the sigmoid (mandibular) notch.

teach.caption: The mandibular canal runs through the body from the mandibular foramen, carrying the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels beneath the lower teeth.

teach.h: The TMJ: a hinge that also slides
teach.body: The TMJ is a synovial joint between the condyle of the mandible and the glenoid (mandibular) fossa of the temporal bone, just in front of the ear. A disc of fibrocartilage sits between them, cushioning the joint and splitting it into upper and lower compartments. Small openings are a hinge movement: the condyle rotates. For a wide opening the condyle and disc also glide forward onto a ridge called the articular eminence.

teach.h: How the jaw opens, and how it dislocates

steps.label: Hinge
steps.sub: Condyle rotates in the fossa: small opening

steps.label: Glide
steps.sub: Condyle and disc slide forward onto the articular eminence

steps.label: Over-opening
steps.sub: Yawning or a long, wide-open appointment

steps.label: Dislocation
steps.sub: Condyle locks in front of the eminence: mouth stuck open

teach.caption: The other movements are protrusion (jaw forward), retrusion (back) and lateral (side to side) movements for grinding.

teach.text: Condyle versus coronoid: the CONDYLE is at the back and makes the joint; the CORONOID is at the front and anchors temporalis. And the MANDIBULAR foramen is on the INSIDE of the ramus, while the MENTAL foramen is on the OUTSIDE of the body.

items: The skull is the cranium plus the facial skeleton; the mandible is its only movable bone.
Maxilla: upper teeth, front of the hard palate, tuberosity and the maxillary sinus.
Mandible: body, ramus, angle, condyle, coronoid process, mandibular and mental foramina.
TMJ: condyle in the glenoid fossa of the temporal bone, with a disc; it hinges, then glides.
Chairside: support the jaw, give rests on long appointments, and tell the dentist about clicking, pain or locking.

summary: You can now name the main bones of the skull, describe the maxilla and its sinus, label the landmarks of the mandible and say why each matters, and explain how the TMJ hinges and glides, and why a wide yawn can leave the jaw locked open.

A.q: A patient's jaw locks open after a wide yawn. Which part of the mandible has moved out of position?
A.why: In dislocation the condyle slides forward past the articular eminence and cannot get back into the glenoid fossa.

whyNot.0: The coronoid process anchors temporalis; it is not part of the jaw joint.
whyNot.1: The angle is where the ramus meets the body; it does not sit in the joint.
whyNot.3: The mental protuberance is the chin, at the front of the mandible.

A.q: The dentist mentions an oro-antral communication after extracting an upper first molar. Which structure has been opened into?
A.why: Upper molar and premolar roots lie close to the floor of the maxillary sinus, so an extraction can leave a hole between mouth and sinus.

whyNot.1: The nasal septum divides the nose; upper molar roots don't reach it.
whyNot.2: The mandibular canal is in the lower jaw and carries the inferior alveolar nerve.
whyNot.3: The glenoid fossa is the socket of the jaw joint in the temporal bone.

A.q: Which bone of the skull contains the socket for the jaw joint?
A.why: The condyle of the mandible sits in the glenoid (mandibular) fossa of the temporal bone.

whyNot.0: The zygomatic bone forms the cheekbone, in front of the joint.
whyNot.1: The sphenoid gives attachment to the pterygoid muscles but does not hold the condyle.
whyNot.2: The maxilla is the upper jaw and does not form part of the TMJ.

options: Outer surface of the body, below the premolars
Inner surface of the body, at the midline
B.why: The mental foramen is on the outer surface of the mandible, usually below the lower premolars, where the mental nerve exits.

whyNot.0: The inner surface of the ramus has the mandibular foramen.
whyNot.2: The inner midline has the genial tubercles for tongue muscles.
whyNot.3: Behind the last upper molar is the maxillary tuberosity.

B.q: Which muscle attaches to the coronoid process of the mandible?
B.why: Temporalis runs from the side of the skull down under the zygomatic arch to insert on the coronoid process.

whyNot.0: Masseter inserts on the outer surface of the ramus and angle.
whyNot.1: Lateral pterygoid inserts on the neck of the condyle and the joint disc.
whyNot.2: Buccinator is the cheek muscle and doesn't attach to the coronoid process.

B.q: What separates the TMJ into an upper and a lower compartment?
B.why: A disc of fibrocartilage lies between the condyle and the fossa, dividing the joint into two compartments.

whyNot.1: The articular eminence is the bony ridge in front of the fossa that the condyle glides onto.
whyNot.2: The sigmoid notch is the dip between the condyle and coronoid process.
whyNot.3: The periodontal ligament holds a tooth in its socket; it is not part of the TMJ.

C.q: Which statement about the mandible is correct?
options: It is fixed to the skull by sutures
It is a pair of bones in adults
It is the only movable skull bone
C.why: The mandible is the only bone of the skull that moves, via the two TMJs.

whyNot.0: Sutures fix the other skull bones; the mandible articulates through synovial joints.
whyNot.1: The two halves fuse at the midline (the symphysis) in early childhood, leaving a single bone.
whyNot.3: The maxillary sinus is in the maxilla, the upper jaw.

C.q: A patient opens slightly to have an upper tooth checked. What movement is happening at the TMJ?
options: The condyle glides onto the eminence
The condyle rotates like a hinge
The disc moves backwards out of the joint
The coronoid process enters the fossa
C.why: Small openings are mainly a hinge (rotation) of the condyle; wider opening adds a forward glide.

whyNot.0: Gliding forward onto the eminence happens on wide opening, not slight opening.
whyNot.2: The disc moves forward with the condyle, and it stays within the joint.
whyNot.3: The coronoid process never enters the fossa; the condyle forms the joint.

C.q: Which landmark is the target area for an inferior dental block injection?
C.why: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen on the inner ramus, so solution is placed near it.

whyNot.0: The mental foramen is where the mental nerve exits, on the outer body of the mandible.
whyNot.1: The incisive foramen is on the palate behind the upper central incisors.
whyNot.2: The infraorbital foramen is on the maxilla below the eye socket.

reteach.title: Picture the lower jaw as a letter 'L' on each side
reteach.question: Hold your hand flat with your thumb pointing up: the fingers are the body of the mandible and the thumb is the ramus. Where are the landmarks?

blocks.body: Start at the chin and run your finger back along the body: the teeth sit on top, and below the premolars on the outside is a small hole, the mental foramen. Where the body turns upwards is the angle. Climb the ramus: at the top front is a pointed tip, the coronoid process, and at the top back is a rounded knob, the condyle, which sits in a socket just in front of your ear. Put a fingertip there and open wide: you can feel it slide forward.

blocks.h: Front of the ramus versus back

blocks.text: Inside versus outside: the MANDIBULAR foramen (in) is on the inner face of the ramus; the MENTAL foramen (out) is on the outer face of the body near the chin.

explain.body: Paired upper jaw bones. They hold the upper teeth, form the front of the hard palate and contain the maxillary sinuses. Upper premolar and molar roots lie close to the sinus floor, so extractions there can open into the sinus.

explain.caption: Extracting 16 carries a risk of an oro-antral communication.

test.q: Which part of the maxilla lies just behind the last upper molar?
test.why: The maxillary tuberosity is the rounded bulge of bone behind the last upper molar.

whyNot.1: The palatine process forms the front of the hard palate.
whyNot.2: The incisive foramen is behind the upper central incisors.
whyNot.3: The coronoid process belongs to the mandible.

explain.body: A horseshoe-shaped body carrying the lower teeth, and a ramus rising on each side. The ramus meets the body at the angle and ends in two processes: the coronoid at the front and the condyle at the back.

test.q: On which part of the mandible is the mandibular foramen found?
test.why: The mandibular foramen is on the inner (medial) surface of the ramus, where the inferior alveolar nerve enters the bone.

whyNot.0: The outer surface of the body has the mental foramen.
whyNot.1: The inner angle gives attachment to medial pterygoid.

explain.h: The two foramina and their nerves
explain.body: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen, runs in the mandibular canal under the lower teeth, and its mental branch leaves through the mental foramen to supply the lower lip and chin. That is why an IDB numbs the lip.

steps.label: Mental foramen
steps.sub: Mental nerve exits to lip and chin

test.q: A patient has a numb lower lip after an IDB. Through which opening did the nerve to the lip leave the bone?
test.why: The mental nerve leaves through the mental foramen to supply the skin and mucosa of the lower lip and chin.

whyNot.0: The mandibular foramen is where the nerve enters the bone, not where the lip branch exits.
whyNot.2: The greater palatine foramen serves the palate.
whyNot.3: The infraorbital foramen serves the upper lip and cheek.

explain.body: A synovial joint between the condyle and the glenoid fossa of the temporal bone, with a fibrocartilage disc. It hinges for small openings and glides forward onto the articular eminence for wide ones. Over-opening can lock the condyle in front of the eminence.

explain.h: TMJ problems a nurse may notice

rows.label: Mouth locked open after a yawn
Tired jaw on a long appointment
rows.tag: Offer a rest or bite block

test.q: During a long root canal treatment, what is the best way to protect the patient's TMJ?
options: Ask them to open as wide as they can
Offer rests and a bite block as directed
Push the jaw backwards between steps
Ask them to keep their teeth clenched
test.why: Short rests and a bite block, used as the dentist directs, reduce strain on the joint and muscles during prolonged opening.

whyNot.0: Maximum opening for a long time strains the joint and risks dislocation.
whyNot.2: Pushing on the jaw is not a nurse's role and could cause injury.
whyNot.3: The patient cannot be treated with teeth clenched, and it does not protect the joint.
